questions.question_text:
A biologist tags $75$ fish in a dam and releases them.
A week later she catches $60$ fish and finds $15$ of them tagged.
Estimate the number of fish in the dam.

options.why: Inverted the proportion, computing $\dfrac{15\times60}{75}$ instead of $\dfrac{75\times60}{15}$.
Multiplied $75\times60$ but never divided by the $15$ tagged fish found in the second catch.
Added the two catches and subtracted the overlap, $75+60-15$, as if the two samples covered the whole dam.

questions.question_text:
A ranger tags $130$ wombats and releases them.
In a later sample of $48$ wombats, $7$ are tagged.
Estimate the wombat population, correct to the nearest whole wombat.

options.why: Rounded $891.43$ up because a part-animal was left over, instead of rounding to the nearest whole number.
Multiplied $130\times48$ but never divided by the $7$ tagged wombats found in the second sample.
Added the two catches and subtracted the overlap, $130+48-7$, instead of using the proportion.

questions.question_text:
A lake is estimated to contain $1200$ eels.
Earlier in the study, $200$ eels were tagged and released.
In a new random sample of $60$ eels, how many would you expect to be tagged?

options.why: Inverted the proportion, computing $\dfrac{1200\times60}{200}$ instead of $\dfrac{200\times60}{1200}$.
Multiplied $200\times60$ without dividing by the population estimate of $1200$.
Divided the population estimate by the number tagged, giving how many eels there are per tagged eel rather than the number tagged in the sample.

questions.question_text:
A conservation team estimates that a colony holds $5400$ penguins.
In a later sample of $180$ penguins, $15$ carry tags from an earlier stage of the study.
How many penguins were tagged in that earlier stage?

options.why: Multiplied $15\times5400$ without dividing by the sample size of $180$.
Divided the population by the sample size, which gives how many such samples fit in the colony, not the number tagged.
Inverted the proportion, computing $\dfrac{180\times5400}{15}$ instead of $\dfrac{15\times5400}{180}$.

questions.question_text:
Between the tagging and the recapture, heavy rain lets many untagged frogs move into the wetland from nearby dams.
Which assumption does this break, and what happens to the population estimate?

options.text: The population must be closed, with no animals moving in or out, and the estimate will be too high.
The population must be closed, with no animals moving in or out, and the estimate will be too low.
options.why: Extra untagged frogs lower the tagged fraction of the second sample, and a lower tagged fraction raises the population estimate rather than lowering it.

options.text: The marks must stay attached to the animals, and the estimate will be too high.
options.why: No marks were lost here; the problem is untagged animals entering the area, which is the closed-population assumption.

options.text: The tagged frogs must mix evenly through the wetland, and the estimate is unaffected.
options.why: Mixing is not what fails here, and adding untagged animals does change the tagged fraction of the sample, so the estimate does change.

questions.solution_text:
The extra untagged frogs mean the wetland is no longer a closed population.
They lower the tagged fraction of the second sample.
A smaller tagged fraction gives a larger population estimate, so the estimate will be too high.

questions.question_text:
Tagged birds learn that the researcher's traps hold food, so they keep returning to the traps.
What effect does this have on the estimated bird population?

options.text: Too low, because more tagged birds than expected appear in the second sample.
Too high, because more tagged birds than expected appear in the second sample.
options.why: More tagged birds raises the tagged fraction of the sample, and a larger tagged fraction gives a smaller population estimate, not a larger one.

options.text: Too high, because fewer tagged birds than expected appear in the second sample.
options.why: Birds that return to the traps are recaptured more often, not less often, so the number of tagged birds found goes up.

options.text: No effect, because the number of birds tagged in the first stage has not changed.
options.why: The estimate depends on the tagged fraction of the second sample, and this behaviour changes that fraction.

questions.solution_text:
Tagged birds are recaptured more often than untagged birds.
This raises the tagged fraction of the second sample.
A larger tagged fraction gives a smaller population estimate, so the estimate will be too low.

questions.question_text:
In the first stage of a study, $84$ turtles were tagged and released.
In the second stage, $21$ of the turtles caught were tagged, and this was $35\%$ of the second catch.
Estimate the turtle population.

options.why: Stopped at the size of the second catch instead of going on to estimate the whole population.
Multiplied $84$ by $35\%$ instead of dividing by it, and did not round to a whole number of animals.
Multiplied $84\times21$, ignoring the $35\%$ that fixes the size of the second catch.

questions.solution_text:
$n=\dfrac{21}{0.35}$
$=60\text{ turtles in the second catch}$
$\dfrac{21}{60}=\dfrac{84}{N}$
$N=\dfrac{84\times60}{21}$
$=\dfrac{5040}{21}$
$=240\text{ turtles}$

questions.question_text:
A capture–recapture study of wallabies in $2023$ tagged $180$ wallabies, and a later sample of $120$ wallabies contained $30$ tagged.
The $2023$ estimate was $20\%$ more than the $2018$ estimate.
What was the estimated wallaby population in $2018$?

options.why: Gave the $2023$ estimate instead of going back to the $2018$ estimate.
Took $20\%$ off the $2023$ figure, $720\times0.8$, instead of dividing by $1.2$ to reverse a $20\%$ increase.
Increased the $2023$ figure by $20\%$ instead of reversing the increase.

questions.question_text:
A farmer wants to estimate the number of rabbits on his farm.
On Monday he catches 120 rabbits, puts a tag on each rabbit, and lets them run away.
On Tuesday he catches 70 rabbits, and 15 of these rabbits have a tag on them.
Which of the following calculations would give the best estimate for the total number of rabbits on the farm?

options.why: This reverses the population relationship and gives a much smaller value.
Dividing the tagged proportion by 120 cannot estimate the population.
This multiplies by the tagged proportion instead of dividing by it.

questions.solution_text: The proportion tagged in the Tuesday sample is $\frac{15}{70}$. Set this equal to the proportion of all rabbits represented by the 120 tagged rabbits. The estimate is $120\div\frac{15}{70}=560$.

questions.question_text:
Clive wants to estimate the number of bees in a beehive.
Clive catches 40 bees from the beehive.
He marks each bee with a dye.
He then lets the bees go.
The next day, Clive catches 50 bees from the beehive. 4 of these bees have been marked with the dye.
Which of the following calculation would give the best estimate for the total number of bees in the hive?

options.why: Divides the marked proportion by the second sample size.
Reverses the population relationship and produces a tiny estimate.
Multiplies the recapture proportion instead of dividing by it.

questions.solution_text: The marked proportion in the second sample is $\frac{4}{50}$. This represents $\frac{40}{N}$ of the whole population, so $N=40\div\frac{4}{50}$.
